channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: AI assistant hacks gym website in first known Australian autonomous cyber attack
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “Andrew asked his personal assistant to book him a spot in one of his gym’s coveted morning classes. … His AI assistant found a way to book the gym class months further in advance than the gym allowed, thanks to a vulnerability it discovered in the booking software. Then it went further, kicking someone out of the waiting list who was ahead of Andrew — something it was not asked to do.”

item.title: New Amazon Data Center Stokes Worry It Would Be the Most Polluting Power Plant in the U.S.
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Amazon is investing in a large-scale natural-gas-burning power plant as part of a huge data center in Texas, the company confirmed on Friday, a facility that could become the largest single source of climate pollution in the United States.”

item.title: OpenAI gives cyber defenders a less-restricted new model
item.description: Axios: “OpenAI is introducing a more cyber-permissive version of GPT-5.6 Sol to vetted defenders as it prepares companies for autonomous cyberattacks. … The move comes just days after OpenAI said it was delaying the release of its forthcoming model, Astra, after it reached critical hacking abilities during safety testing.”

item.title: A.I. Agents Are Taking Entire Online Courses for Cheating Students
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Sometimes students can earn full degrees online. In other cases, they take individual classes. In this realm, A.I. cheating is quickly accelerating beyond the copy-and-pasting of chatbot-produced essays and problem sets. A.I. agents have made it possible for students to outsource a semester of work.”

item.title: Data center operator CyrusOne plans potential 2027 IPO, banks pitch for roles, sources say
item.description: Reuters: “CyrusOne, a data center operator owned by KKR (KKR.N) and BlackRock’s (BLK.N) Global Infrastructure Partners, is preparing for an initial public offering as early as ​2027, in what could be one of the biggest IPOs in the ‌sector in recent years, according to people familiar with the matter.”

item.title: Andy Beshear defends Kentucky data center order
item.description: Forward Kentucky: “Gov. Andy Beshear is defending an executive order aimed at regulating data center development in Kentucky, saying it is designed to protect ratepayers and the environment while allowing projects to move forward where communities support them.”

item.title: Anthropic pledges to embed watermarks to help discern AI slop in sop to EU
item.description: The Register: “Anthropic will embed watermarks in the text and files generated by future models it launches in the EU, as part of its effort to comply with content and transparency rules in the bloc’s AI Act.”

item.title: The AI industry won a primary fight. Now its target is inspiring lawmakers nationwide.
item.description: Politico: “A super PAC network backed by artificial intelligence executives hoped to make an example of Alex Bores when it targeted him for defeat in a Democratic House primary over his authorship of a New York AI law. Instead, the New York State assemblymember has emerged as an inspiration and a source of ideas for state lawmakers nationwide who are pushing for rules to rein in AI — despite losing a congressional primary in June under an $8 million barrage of pro-tech attacks.”

item.title: Mark Zuckerberg Posts Deranged 6,500-Word Essay About Giving Everyone AI Superintelligence
item.description: 404 Media: “Zuckerberg lays out the potential use case for Meta glasses (whose huge marketing campaign cannot get people to stop calling them ‘pervert glasses’), AI agents, open weights AI development, and why data centers are not bad for communities, actually. Like most Silicon Valley ‘utopian’ essays, to believe that any of this is going to go how Zuckerberg suggests it will requires one to have been recently concussed or to willfully ignore how this technology is being used today and believe that thousands of years of human nature will suddenly shift.”

item.title: Roku Unleashes 24/7 AI Slop Channel
item.description: Futurism: “In one clip that gives an idea of the bottom-of-the-barrel slop that it’s force feeding viewers, we see an AI movie that’s apparently meant to be some sort of medieval drama, only with laggy physics that makes it look like it takes place on the Moon. If there is a plot, it’s masterfully hidden underneath the bizarre way it cuts to different scenes, not to mention dialog that’s delivered with the cadence and awkward pauses of a mid-2000s video game cutscene. No one blinks when they talk.”

item.title: Spotify to Start Labeling AI Artists
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “Spotify has announced a new feature intended to label AI artist profiles on the platform, one of the company’s most significant moves to date as the streamer looks to offer users more transparency about AI content on the service.”

item.title: How AI is being used to track art stolen by the Nazis
item.description: NPR: “During World War II, the Nazis looted more than 600,000 works of art, mostly owned by Jews. In the decades since, there’s been an effort to get these works back to their owners, but it’s not easy, and roughly a fifth of them have still not been returned. Now, a new AI chatbot might be making that complicated process a little simpler.”

item.title: Could Nevada’s tech epicenter run out of water? That’s the big question in an ongoing suit
item.description: The Nevada Independent: “A bitter legal battle has emerged over water availability in Nevada’s technology epicenter, raising questions about whether companies critical to diversifying the state economy have enough water to survive into the future.”

item.title: Study: ChatGPT ads appear on 26% of commercial prompts
item.description: Search Engine Land: “SE Ranking found sponsored placements on 25.94% of commercial prompts, putting ChatGPT surprisingly close to Google’s AI Mode, where the company’s previous research found ads on 29.45% of commercial queries.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Bengal’s revolutionary legacy finds a digital home in BRIL Virtual Museum
item.description: The Statesman: “Seeking to preserve Bengal’s revolutionary legacy in an engaging and accessible format, banker and researcher Boddhisatya Tarafdar has launched the Bengal Revolution for India’s Liberation (BRIL) Virtual Museum, a digital archive that traces the state’s defining role in India’s fight against British colonial rule.”

item.title: NEW ONLINE TOOL: 2026 ‘Electronic Waste Graveyard’ highlights growing issues of trashed tech products
item.description: US PIRG: “U.S. PIRG Education Fund on Tuesday launched its updated online Electronic Waste Graveyard. This interactive digital database reveals how many otherwise-usable smart appliances, phones and other connected devices that people have to trash because the software has expired or lost support.”

item.title: Take a look at Marilyn Monroe’s lipstick in the first makeup archive of its kind
item.description: Bangkok Post: “What do Marilyn Monroe, celluloid powder and cosmetics dating back to the 17th century have in common? They can now be found under one digital roof. Makeup artist and beauty historian Erin Parsons has launched The Makeup Archive, an online museum dedicated to preserving the history of cosmetics.”

item.title: Google Play adds Venmo as a payment option
item.description: TechCrunch: “Google Play already offers other digital payment methods including PayPal and Cash App along with cards from American Express, Visa, Mastercard, Discover and JCB in the United States. Outside the U.S., the company has also experimented with allowing users to pay for digital purchases using cash at a nearby store.”

item.title: 4 free tools that find what’s wrong with your internet in minutes
item.description: MakeUseOf: “If your Wi-Fi has been flaky lately — buffering during video calls, lagging in games, or just feeling slower than usual — there are a few settings you should check before blaming your ISP. But changing settings is one thing; knowing what to change them to is another. Slow speeds or an intermittent connection are big enough problems for you to know that there’s something wrong with your internet. If you want to know exactly what’s wrong, there are tons of free tools out there that can help you out.”

item.title: 11 best alternative search engines to Google in 2026
item.description: Search Engine Watch: “In recent years, Google has made significant changes that have particularly impacted publishers and other content creators. At the same time, we’ve witnessed the rise of alternative search engines. Although Google continues to dominate the market, there are many reasons you might consider exploring other options. We’ve compiled and tested a list of alternatives in our environment.”

item.title: Top Creators’ Secret Weapon? Indian Video Editors
item.description: Hollywood Reporter: “Mega-popular creators like Dude Perfect, former NASA engineer Mark Rober, and chef Nick DiGiovanni have all hired remote editors from across the world, according to Sina Sahami, the CEO of YT Jobs, a LinkedIn, of sorts, for YouTubers. These remote gigs are particularly appealing to international youngsters who wander the world, bopping from country to country.”

item.title: As AI grips world, the thrill of collecting vintage computers is growing
item.description: Associated Press: “While Silicon Valley has since moved on to shaping the future of artificial intelligence, these hardware enthusiasts are intent on saving the Atari, Commodore and IBM machines that are ancestors to today’s laptops, wearable devices and smart phones. Where others see junk, people like [Josh] Dersch see artifacts of computer history that are worthy of attention and respect.”

item.title: Rising number of UK children report seeing explicit deepfakes of themselves
item.description: The Guardian: “The Report Remove service, which blocks intimate images from appearing online, said there had been a rapid increase in imagery that had been digitally manipulated or ‘faked’ in some way, including with AI and nudification tools. In the first six months of this year it received 420 reports from children of images of themselves that they believed had been faked or manipulated to appear explicit. The number has already exceeded its 2025 total of 397.”

item.title: Millions of burnt books show how ‘war of endurance’ is hurting Ukraine
item.description: Reuters: “A Russian drone strike ​on Ranok’s warehouse in the northeastern city of Kharkiv on August 1 destroyed about 8 million books, the biggest blow yet to Ukraine’s publishing industry during ‌the four-year-old war. Publishers say more than 10 million books have been destroyed in attacks on warehouses in recent months, threatening an industry that initially benefited from rising demand for Ukrainian-language literature at the start of the conflict.”

item.title: Launch of Virtual Reference Service for Archival Access
item.description: Richard Nixon Presidential Library: “The Richard Nixon Presidential Library and Museum announces the launch of its new Virtual Reference Service (VRS), designed to provide researchers with remote access to archival materials. This innovative service allows users to engage with historical documents through scheduled, staff-mediated sessions conducted virtually.”

item.title: New Issues of The Sylva Herald and Ruralite Reveal History of Female Publishers in the 20th Century
item.description: DigitalNC: “Thanks to our partners at Southwestern Community College and Jackson County Public Library, along with funding from the Library Services and Technology Act, new issues from 1951 to 1980 of The Sylva Herald and Ruralite (Sylva, N.C.) are now available online at DigitalNC!”

item.title: Stephen Petronio Company to Launch Digital Archive of 40-Year Legacy
item.description: Broadway World: “The Stephen Petronio Company has announced the launch of a digital archive dedicated to preserving and celebrating the artistic legacy of the Company. Designed as a dynamic online resource, the archive features videos, photographs, interviews, timeline, and other media, offering an intimate look at the breadth of Stephen Petronio’s practice and the Company’s history.”

item.title: DC’s care networks are an urban feature. Governance needs to catch up
item.description: Greater Greater Washington: “Who is already doing the work of producing health equity in the district, and how does governance support that work? That question is a recurring theme in the DC Voices of Care oral history project, part of Georgetown University’s Global Cities Initiative. The project documents the experiences of community and organizational leaders whose work, through their organizations and networks, has shaped the conditions that influence health and care across Washington, DC over several decades. ”

item.title: I built my own Wayback Machine, and now I never lose web pages
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Webpage archive tools like The Wayback Machine have rescued me from plenty of dead links, but it has one weakness that is unfortunately unavoidable. It can only recover a page if someone was thoughtful enough to archive it before it disappeared. I wanted a private version where I chose what sites to snapshot, capture them in advance, and keep several recoverable formats on hardware that I controlled. So, I installed ArchiveBox on an Ubuntu virtual machine and started building my own little private corner of internet history.”

item.title: For vertical live streamers, YouTube is stressing that practice makes perfect
item.description: Tubefilter: “Nearly a year after it was first teased, Practice Mode for Vertical Live is here. That’s the name of a new feature that provides a trial run for streaming greenhorns who are looking to go live more often.”

item.title: Google says Reddit gets no special preference in search
item.description: Search Engine Watch: “Google communications representative Jennifer Kutz confirmed to The Verge that Reddit gets no preferential treatment in Google’s search rankings or AI search features.”

item.title: Emily Dickinson Museum tour guides negotiate first union contract a year after Amherst vote
item.description: Daily Hampshire Gazette: “A year after voting to unionize, part-time tour guides and educators at the Emily Dickinson Museum, who throughout the spring, summer and fall are leading visitors through the historic homes and grounds that inspired the 19th century poet, are in the midst of negotiating their first contract.”

item.title: Three in five Americans favor stronger oversight of social media companies, Reuters/Ipsos poll finds
item.description: Reuters: “A bipartisan majority of Americans support more government rules for how ​social media companies conduct business, including a requirement of age-verification tools to keep younger children off social media, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll.”

item.title: Infiltrating the Jennifer Aniston Twitter Bot Squad
item.description: Jezebel: “In case you slept through the last decade, the website formerly known as Twitter has devolved into something of a patient zero for dead internet theory. In other words, it’s pretty much just bots, with a side of Poo Crave and Elon Musk. An article published in The New Yorker last week cited a study estimating that, in a sample of more than 1 million Twitter accounts, 64% were likely bots. And after taking several strolls through the dark halls of this hellsite, I now believe that Jennifer Aniston is responsible. Or rather, the fellowship of catfishing bots posing as Jennifer Aniston is responsible.”

item.title: Track Bird Visitors With A Raspberry Pi And A USB Mic
item.description: Hackaday: “Avian Visitors is a lovely project by [Teddy Warner] that uses a Raspberry Pi and microphone to keep track of which birds have been visiting your home, and creates a colorful illustration of recent visitors on top of it all. It reports on a web interface of its own making, but what really takes things to a new level is an optional, stylish E-Ink panel that shows the last 24 hours’ worth of visitors at a glance in a collage.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Newsroom Guide for Authentication and Verification in the AI Age
item.description: CITP Blog: “At our June workshop, organized jointly by Princeton’s Center for Information Technology Policy (CITP) and NYU Journalism, participants shared a desire for a practical, short-form resource to help newsrooms understand the current landscape of authentication and verification tools for addressing AI-generated content. To complement our full report, we have translated the workshop discussions into a short guide on considerations for newsroom workflows. The newsroom guide is now available online.”

item.title: VJC launches digital archive showcasing decades of jazz history
item.description: The Commons: “For nearly three decades, under the direction of Eugene Uman and Elsa Borrero, the Vermont Jazz Center archive team has documented concerts, masterclasses, interviews, and educational programs. These historically significant gems include recent events as well as the special collection of VJC founder Attila Zoller that features recorded performances from as early as the mid-1950s.”

item.title: Made by Google 2026: What to Expect From the Pixel 11 Event
item.description: Lifehacker: “Almost a full year has passed since the launch of Google’s Pixel 10 phones, which of course means it’s time for the Pixel 11 handsets to make their debut. Another Made by Google event has been scheduled for Wednesday, Aug. 12, with everything getting underway in New York from 6 pm EDT / 3 pm PDT.”

item.title: Meet the army of amateur archivists racing to save US history in national parks
item.description: The Guardian: “Hundreds of volunteers, many of whom are anonymous, have submitted photos of national signage to the digital archive. As of 3 August, the site has compiled 17,236 photos, including at least one in nearly every national park and historic site in the country.”

item.title: A Quieter Place: Why textlog Reminds Me of the Twitter I Actually Miss
item.description: Herlein: “I was pleasantly surprised to come across textlog, a small, new project that seems to be trying to rebuild that room on purpose. The pitch, in the site’s own words, is ‘a quieter place for your thoughts.’ That’s not marketing copy dressed up as humility — it’s an actual design constraint.”

item.title: How Russia is impersonating French news outlets in a bid to influence France’s next presidential election
item.description: Meduza: “Russian disinformation networks have launched an active campaign to interfere in France’s presidential election, which is set for April 2027. Over the past two weeks, at least three cases have come to light in which these networks spread fake news about possible candidates on social media, including by posing as popular French outlets.”

item.title: Cruise ship helps stranded skiff and crew in Southeast Alaska as Zuckerberg yacht stands by
item.description: Alaska Beacon: “A small cruise ship operating in Southeast Alaska made an unexpected detour on Monday night to help a 21-foot skiff that ran out of fuel between Petersburg and Juneau. Michael Love, a software developer from New York City, was a passenger aboard the cruise ship and described the event on social media. What got his attention the most wasn’t the rescue itself — it was when the captain announced that the yacht of billionaire Facebook owner Mark Zuckerberg was closer and hadn’t answered the radio call for help.”

item.title: TikTok withheld a safety feature from 15 million users, report says
item.description: Mashable: “A confidential internal document obtained by Bloomberg Aug. 4 found that TikTok excluded 10 percent of its U.S. users from an algorithmic safety update in early 2022. At the time, that would have amounted to roughly 15 million people. Among them was Chase Nasca, a 16-year-old from Long Island who died by suicide in Feb. 2022.”

item.title: Intrusion at US healthcare software provider puts 3.8M people’s data at risk
item.description: The Register: “A US healthcare software provider has admitted that hackers may have made off with sensitive data belonging to 3.8 million people, making it the largest healthcare breach reported to regulators so far this year.”

item.title: Sacred, historic Ohio sites could have weakened protections under proposed federal regulations
item.description: WYSO: “A federal advisory council is proposing sweeping changes to regulations intended to protect historic sites. The proposed regulations could prevent historic Ohio tribes from saving their sacred sites.”

item.title: From Archive to Dataset: AI-Assisted Mass Digitisation of Historical Photographic Collections, Using the Sven Simon Archive as a Case Study
item.description: Digital Meets Culture: “The objective is not merely to preserve individual images, but to transform entire collection contexts into structured, searchable datasets. The first large-scale implementation is the Sven Simon Archive, comprising approximately 1.6 million photographs relating to German and international political, cultural, economic and sporting history since the early 1960s.”

item.title: Mapping Monsters: SDSS-V Data Release 20 Unveils All-Sky Views of Supermassive Black Holes
item.description: SDSS: “The Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) announces Data Release 20 (DR20), marking a landmark expansion in the study of accreting supermassive black holes (SMBHs).” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: RELEASE: Community repair events popping up across country: new online tool helps you find them
item.description: This was from June but I missed it! PIRG: “Frustrated by our throwaway culture, people around the world are organizing free repair events. These gatherings, which are called Repair Cafes, Fixit Clinics and other names, allow people to connect and help each other fix broken items instead of replacing them. Now, there’s an easy way to find one of these events near you. On Tuesday, U.S. PIRG Education Fund and iFixit announced the opening of the Community Repair Hub, the first nationwide registry of upcoming community repair events.”

item.title: Dabbers club historian launches online archive preserving more than 140 years of club history
item.description: Nantwitch Town FC: “As Nantwich Town prepare to kick off another football season, supporters can now take a journey through more than 140 years of the club’s remarkable past thanks to the launch of a comprehensive new online archive. The free ‘DABBERSarchive’ website brings together thousands of historic records, photographs, match reports and player profiles, creating the most complete digital record ever assembled of the Cheshire club’s long and proud history.”

item.title: Maproom Blog
item.description: Spotted on Reading Maps. From the About page: “Reading Maps came out of a nagging thought that every story has happened somewhere. Odysseus crossed a real sea. The Pequod sailed real water. Phileas Fogg’s eighty days ran on real railways and real steamer lines and that you could follow him in a way. However when you read a book, all that geography stays locked in your head. Once you close the cover and it goes with it. So I started plotting them properly. Real coastlines, real ports, one journey at a time.”

item.title: Remembering the pre-Google web, when search was an experiment
item.description: Ars Technica: “In the mid-’90s, the web was exploding, but finding anything of actual value on it felt like an elaborate negotiation with whatever proto-search engine happened to be standing closest to the door. Unlike now, when Google is widely seen as both portal and gatekeeper, sites like AltaVista, Lycos, Excite, HotBot, and Ask Jeeves promised to tame the chaos, each with its own suite of quirks, charms, and flaws.”

item.title: HRC condemns DoE removal of LGBTQ+ bullying data from federal survey
item.description: Los Angeles Blade: “The Human Rights Campaign is slamming the White House — and the Department of Education — following their removal of some LGBTQ+ bullying data from federal data collection.”

item.title: Restaurants, pubs and theatres ban Meta’s ‘spy glasses’ over privacy fears
item.description: The Guardian: “When Meta used superstar Kylie Jenner to promote its sleek new line of ‘spy glasses’, the social media company hoped the devices would reach the same broad acceptance that tablets and smartwatches have found before them. But those plans have hit a snag in the UK, where venues from elite restaurants to popular pub chains have banned the £359 glasses in order to preserve the privacy of customers and staff.” Posterity, nobody is calling these things “spy glasses.” We are calling them “pervert glasses.”

item.title: The Cossack crosses at Odessa’s oldest cemetery will be digitized and displayed on a map
item.description: Intent: “An international project has been launched in Odesa to study and digitally preserve the Kuyalnik Cossack Cemetery, which is considered the oldest in the city. As part of the project, an open online platform and an interactive map will be created, and a digital album featuring stone Cossack crosses will be published.”

item.title: Dark personality traits linked to problematic social media use via jealousy and cyberstalking
item.description: PsyPost: “A recent study published in Current Psychology indicates that individuals with antagonistic personality traits tend to develop problematic social media habits driven by jealousy and a desire to monitor their romantic partners online.”

item.title: FIT and Columbia Work Together on a New Sustainable Fiber
item.description: FIT: “FIT, in partnership with Columbia University, has been awarded an $11.5 million grant from the Bezos Earth Fund to develop a high-performance, sustainable textile fiber grown by bacteria.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Google’s AI somehow knew a game secret that existed only in a private Google Doc
item.description: TechSpot: “What we know so far: After a player asked Google’s AI about unreleased content in his game, an indie developer says it returned a character name that existed only in a private Google Doc. Klub Kofta Studio, the solo developer behind the tower defense game Operation Octo, said the character, called Vantage Tripod, had not been announced or shared with anyone.”

item.title: Ooops! Developer blames AI mapping for showing wrong house at abutter’s meeting
item.description: Dorchester Reporter: “A developer’s plan to demolish a single-family home at 59 Gibson Street and replace it with a 4-story, multi-unit building took an unexpected turn Monday evening after neighbors pointed out that the renderings and plans he was presenting to a public abutters meeting were highly questionable, given that they showed a three-decker house.”

item.title: Protesters haul a guillotine to city council meeting about a potential AI data center, company rep cornered by protestors — ‘ it no longer felt safe to stay,’ developer escorted out by police
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “The Salem City Council convened a public meeting last July 27, where it discussed the proposed $5.1 billion Oakline at Mill Creek data center by Verrus. As the people converged on the meeting site, a TikTok user spotted a guillotine towed by a bike outside of the venue, signaling the people’s discontent with the project.”

item.title: Eric Adams Is Selling Data Centers in Wisconsin Now
item.description: Hellgate NYC: “A video taken on Saturday afternoon shows Adams in sales pitch mode at the Wisconsin Rapids municipal library, as he’s heckled and shouted down by community members who are opposed to the data center, which is being proposed by the PNK Group.”

item.title: Authorities mum on increased energy use by Keystone Avenue data center
item.description: This is Reno: “Concerned citizens’ emails in June flooded the This Is Reno inbox, along with a five-page list of issues surrounding Centra’s RNO2 data center on Keystone Avenue. Fourteen members of the city council, the planning commission and other city and planning staff also reportedly received dozens of emails from people concerned about the Keystone data center.”

item.title: Anatomy of a secret Coastal Georgia data center deal
item.description: The Current Georgia: “Last fall, representatives of Georgia’s largest utility company assumed the role of matchmaker. They contacted Effingham County officials with a proposal: One of the largest tech companies in the world was looking for a location to build a data center. The ensuing courtship, brokered by Georgia Power and conducted in secret, culminated some nine months later, when OpenAI and Effingham County’s development authority signed a $20 billion deal to construct a data center on a 1,400-acre tract of land near Rincon. Separately, the power company also forged a new contract with OpenAI.”

item.title: As Colorado universities align with ChatGPT, student AI resisters take a stand against the ‘plagiarism machine’
item.description: Denver Post: “Mirakle Wright thought her peers’ opposition to generative artificial intelligence in a world increasingly beset with the technology evoked the convictions held by wartime pacifists. ‘People have such negative feelings about AI. They’re becoming resisters — conscientious objectors,’ said Wright, a University of Colorado Boulder graduate student.”

item.title: ‘I hate what AI is doing to the minds and happiness of the young’: Katherine Rundell on the view from the classroom
item.description: The Guardian: “Going into schools, I meet thousands of children a year and every day I become more certain that, if justice for all is to be our organising principle, AI is not for children and not for young people. It risks becoming an iron curtain that comes down between a young person and their potential for thinking, for experiment and conquering frustration, for stamina and for invention – and thereby, between the young people and their freedom. It risks halting learning before it can take flight.”

item.title: Research, edits and Thurgood Marshall’s voice: How Syracuse officials are using AI
item.description: Central Current: “As Syracusans grow more attuned to the private sector’s increasing use of AI, Central Current asked the city and Common Council if and how elected officials and their staffers are using AI. In a statement to Central Current, Mayor Sharon Owens said AI represents an opportunity to enhance municipal operations, so long as it is implemented in full accordance with city policies. Owens stressed the importance of maintaining public trust while trying to leverage AI.”

item.title: Egypt, UK to launch AI center to help preserve cultural heritage
item.description: Government of Egypt: “The National Research Institute of Astronomy and Geophysics (NRIAG) will inaugurate a joint Egyptian-British center on August 17 aimed at using artificial intelligence and virtual heritage technologies to preserve cultural heritage and advance scientific research, the institute said.”

item.title: Warner Bros. Uses AI Dog Podcast to Promote ‘The End of Oak Street’: ‘Ewan McGregor Was Excellent With Treats’
item.description: Variety: “The 90-second podcast clip, hosted by an AI golden retriever named Goldie and an AI French bulldog named Frenchie, features an interview with Starbuck, who plays Anne Hathaway and Ewan McGregor’s dog in ‘Oak Street.’ Starbuck, of course, is also animated using uncanny AI effects.”

item.title: The new AI billboard locals actually like
item.description: Gazetteer San Francisco: “They said it couldn’t be done: Someone put up an AI ad that locals actually like! Last week, a billboard appeared at the corner of Sixth and Shipley Streets, just off Folsom, advertising ChatTJB, a new chatbot powered by AI (read: ‘average individual’). Tucker Bryant, a keynote speaker and former Google product manager, is the man behind ChatTJB…”

item.title: While American AI Models Race to Commit Felonies, China’s Kimi Broke Out and… Just Used GitHub
item.description: Gizmodo: “Kimi K3, the new model from Chinese AI lab Moonshot, has become the latest AI system to jump the proverbial fence during a routine test, according to a blog post published Thursday by US cybersecurity research startup Frontier Security.”

item.title: When human knowledge has been exhausted, where will AI get its data?
item.description: Northeastern University: “As AI large language models, or LLMs, grow in power and sophistication, where will their architects turn when, someday — as experts predict — algorithms outgrow the limits of general human knowledge and begin craving information possessed by only the world’s most elite thinkers and creators?”

item.title: Stanford is running 37,000 AI agents as a virtual biotech — and one of its drug designs got independently confirmed by Merck
item.description: VentureBeat: “For developers, the operating assumption has been one engineer, one agent — the model Claude Code and similar tools. At VB Transform 2026, James Zou, associate professor of biomedical data science at Stanford University, argued that assumption is about to break: the next frontier isn’t a single, more capable agent, it’s tens of thousands of them collaborating.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: IGFA Announces the E.K. Harry Digital Archive, a Landmark Effort to Preserve the World’s Sportfishing Memory
item.description: International Game Fish Association: “The International Game Fish Association (IGFA) has announced the launch of the E.K. Harry Digital Archive, an ambitious multi-year initiative to digitize, catalog, and preserve the holdings of the E.K. Harry Library of Fishes, the most significant single-topic collection of sportfishing history in the world. When complete, the project will make millions of unique assets, from expedition scrapbooks and historic photographs to world record documents and rare films, searchable on a modern digital platform for the first time.”

item.title: Department of War Publishes Fifth Release of Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Files on WAR.GOV/UFO
item.description: US Government: “Today, the Department of War is publishing the fifth release of declassified and historical Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) files as part of the Presidential Unsealing and Reporting System for UAP Encounters (PURSUE). The collection continues to be housed on WAR.GOV/UFO, and the Department will release additional files on a rolling basis.”

item.title: Vanderbilt’s Art in the Christian Tradition database launches major update
item.description: Vanderbilt University: “Vanderbilt Divinity Library has launched a comprehensive redesign of its Art in the Christian Tradition (ACT) website, fully integrating this database of more than 7,000 religious images with the Revised Common Lectionary (RCL) platform to support digital scholarship and worship. The updated resource features improved search functionality, an IIIF viewer for detailed image analysis, and a commitment to diverse representation.”

item.title: Russia-linked accounts spread far-right narrative online during Ceuta migration crisis, analysis finds
item.description: The Guardian: “Russia-linked social media accounts frequently spread destabilising narratives in Europe, often promoting far-right talking points about immigration. But 411 and other experts suggest the scale and coordination of the disinformation that followed the Ceuta crisis is significant. Groups spreading disinformation are more organised and powerful than they were several years ago.”

item.title: Free Speech and the IndieWeb
item.description: Brennan Day: “A couple days ago, I wrote the blog post titled ‘Five Interesting Indie Platforms You Might Not Have Heard Of’. I was really happy with it—being able to share the work of others that deserve support and can help foster digital indie communities. But, regrettably, I had to rescind one of my recommendations. Let me explain.”

item.title: X is replacing revenue sharing with a new original content rewards program
item.description: Engadget: “The website describes original content as users’ original writing or reporting, photos or videos they take and memes or illustrations they create. They can earn from other people’s posts, but they will have to add meaningful commentary or analysis to them, or to do some creative editing to existing videos or photos.”

item.title: Here’s how newsrooms are working with influencers
item.description: Poynter: “I’ve been watching a growing number of organizations explore collaborations between journalists and creators with great interest.”

item.title: Judge throws out DOE’s blanket ‘still interested’ FOIA policy
item.description: Federal News Network: “A federal judge has tossed out the Energy Department’s proposed policy that would have required people to re-confirm their interest in older Freedom of Information Act requests. In an Aug. 5 order, U.S. District Judge Amy Berman Jackson vacated Energy’s ‘Still Interested Inquiry’ notice from nearly a year ago.”

item.title: ‘They Are Thieves’: FTC Complaints About Hims & Hers Detail Surprise Charges
item.description: Gizmodo: “Last week, the FTC filed a lawsuit against telehealth company Hims & Hers for allegedly disclosing private health information to third parties and engaging in shady subscription practices. Gizmodo filed a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request with the FTC for consumer complaints against the company, which help give an idea of just how prevalent these practices are.”

item.title: AI slop, privacy fears, and endless scrolling are making people fall out of love with the internet
item.description: TechSpot: “More than 50% of participants believe that it’s inevitable their personal data will be breached, with only 11% disagreeing with the statement. Gen Z (born between 1997 and 2012) were most confident they’d be safe, but a still-high 47% believe their data is bound to be hijacked. Gen X (born 1965 to 1980) were most pessimistic (56%).”

item.title: ‘Kids Are Actually Eating the Food’: State Expands Lunch Program That Pairs Schools with Farms
item.description: Santa Barbara Independent: “In school lunchrooms around Lake Tahoe, students line up for a red, hairy fruit called a rambutan. On pozole day, they shout, “We want more!” And when the salad bar runs dry, they ask the staff to refill it – over and over. This brings joy to the cafeteria crew, but Gage Gautheier recently bestowed the highest possible praise from a middle-schooler: ‘I have literally never heard anyone complain about the food.'” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: AI Note-Taking Apps Are Violating User Privacy
item.description: Lifehacker: “A few years ago, AI note-taking and transcription tools were a niche productivity hack used by busy executives and the media. Now, they’re everywhere. But these apps come with a legal fine print that most people don’t know to look for.”

item.title: AI failed to properly patch software flaws 74% of the time, 1Password’s study warns
item.description: ZDNet: “The Off-By-1-Labs started with a hypothesis: frontier AI models would be able to produce ‘reasonably high patch success rates’ — perhaps around 67% success — when they were tasked to develop patches for software, given the open hand of open source code and public disclosures likely included in training these models. However, researchers were probably left disappointed with the results, as they were ‘significantly lower and more uneven than we hypothesized.'”

item.title: Eastport residents fill hearings to oppose underwater AI data‑center plan
item.description: Bangor Daily News: “Washington County residents gathered Wednesday to air fears and frustrations over Eastport’s economic and environmental future at the first of two public hearings on citizen‑initiated ordinances that could halt early preparations for an underwater artificial intelligence data center in the Bay of Fundy’s Western Passage.”

item.title: Inside the secretive deal for a $10 billion data center in rural North Carolina
item.description: NC Newsline: “Steel skeletons of two-story buildings jut from the landscape strewn with building supplies, the site of a $10 billion Amazon data center touted as the largest economic development project in state history. Yet many residents vehemently oppose it. Richmond County officials secretly crafted the deal, which includes significant tax breaks for Amazon, then sprung it on an area already encumbered by pollution.”

item.title: New Mexico environment department updates public comment portal following fraud reports
item.description: Source New Mexico: “The New Mexico Environment Department on Friday announced a change to its public comment portal, following reports of fraudulent submissions in support of a controversial data center’s air quality permits. Source New Mexico reported in June that residents from three New Mexico cities said their names falsely appeared on letters urging state environment officials to approve air quality permits for the Project Jupiter data center after they were approached by canvassers for the project.”

item.title: Dev proves LLMs will run on anything – even a $10 microcontroller
item.description: The Register: “In a process detailed on GitHub, and recently showcased on the Better Stack YouTube channel, SlvDev documented how he managed to get a small language model running at nearly 10 tokens a second locally on a microcontroller that costs about the same as a fancy cup of coffee.”

item.title: Better Hope You Don’t Need an Ambulance in New Orleans, Because the City’s 911 Operators Are Now AI
item.description: Futurism: “If you thought AI customer service bots were bad, just wait until you need to convince a large language model that yes, you have been involved in a car accident, actually. According to new reporting by the Shreveport Times, officials at the Orleans Parish Communication District — the emergency dispatch agency for the city of New Orleans — are now integrating AI answering agents into its workflow.”

item.title: Florida Democrats press DeSantis administration for details about AI contract for SNAP
item.description: Florida Phoenix: “Florida Democrats want to know how the state plans to use artificial intelligence to lower its error rate in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP). To help the state lower its error rate and avoid having to contribute as much as $1 billion toward food costs next year under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, the Florida Legislature appropriated $4 million to the Department of Children and Families in the state fiscal year 2026-27 for AI.”

item.title: Ohio General Assembly members propose sweeping bill to regulate data center development
item.description: Ohio Capital Journal: “In the face of concerns about the environmental, aesthetic, and public finance ramifications of Ohio’s rapid growth in data center development, Ohio House Bill 983 introduces a range of interventions designed to insert the public into data center development decisions.”

item.title: Retailers tap AI shopping traffic but fight to keep customer data
item.description: Reuters: “Growing online traffic ‌from AI platforms has pushed retailers including Walmart, Ulta Beauty and Wayfair to update their websites so their products rank highly in chatbot searches. Yet many want purchases to remain on their own websites, where they can collect data on browsing habits, basket sizes and past purchases that help drive future sales and customer loyalty.”

item.title: AI-assisted staging draws boos at the Richard Wagner festival in Germany
item.description: Associated Press: ” An experiment with artificial intelligence at the annual Richard Wagner festival in the southeastern German town of Bayreuth drew boos from the audience after producing a staging that appeared to leave some spectators confused.”

item.title: No One Knows What the Hell Elon Musk’s AI Graph Means
item.description: Gizmodo: “Elon Musk posted a graph to X on Sunday that has left people scratching their heads. At first glance, it appears Musk is trying to make the case that AI is revolutionary, and it’s no secret the SpaceX CEO believes AI will change the world. But if you actually look at the graph, it’s unclear what the hell it’s supposed to represent.”

item.title: Apple Faces $32.5 Billion Lawsuit Over Facial Recognition in iPhone Photos App
item.description: PetaPixel: “Apple is facing a lawsuit seeking up to $32.5 billion over claims its iPhone Photos app illegally collected users’ biometric information. The iPhone is widely known for using Face ID as a biometric security feature to help protect users’ privacy. However, a class action lawsuit in Illinois alleges that Apple violated privacy laws by collecting biometric data through the Photos app.”

item.title: AI models nearly erase female characters when they write kids stories about animals
item.description: University of Washington: “…for a new study, the researchers gave six leading AI models variations on the same prompt they gave human participants. Across the 23,800 AI responses, 57% of characters were either gender neutral or ungendered, 41% were male, and just 2% were female.”

item.title: Opinion | Mississippi Is Tired of Being Kept in the Dark on Data Centers
item.description: Mississippi Free Press: “Hours after the Jackson City Council voted to pause data center development for six months, Mississippi Gov. Tate Reeves took to social media to mock people who support data center moratoriums as ‘idiots’ who are surrendering America’s technological future to China. That response tells Mississippians almost everything they need to know about the problem.” Good evening, Internet…

item.title: Harpswell Anchor launches archives website
item.description: Harpswell Anchor: “The archives of the Harpswell Anchor, from its first edition in July 1998 through June 2026, are now available in a searchable database at harpswell.historyarchives.online. The website is the culmination of an effort to digitize and preserve years of Anchor archives previously unavailable to the public. It also allows readers to search the archives of the ‘old Anchor,’ for the years 1998-2020, for the first time since the newspaper’s sale in 2021.”

item.title: Shutting Down EchoFeed
item.description: Robb Knight: “I’m shutting down EchoFeed within the next 12 months when the final subscriptions expire. It will continue to run as it is until then so if you’ve already paid you have access until the end of your subscription.”

item.title: TikTok quickly pauses dating live chat test
item.description: Mashable: “TikTok has paused a test of a dating feature that put singles in live chats, Business Insider reported. Over the past week, TikTok tested the tool, which was in a section of the app called ‘hangout.'”

item.title: Netflix Making Kids’ Shows More Accessible
item.description: Disability Scoop: “Through a new arrangement, Netflix will make hundreds of hours of programing for kids and families more accessible to those with disabilities. Starting this week, the streaming service will add overlays with Deaf performers interpreting in American Sign Language to 73 titles.”

item.title: Mondo Metrics says its new trend tracker is “what CrowdTangle would have become”–and it’s launching with major sports leagues
item.description: Tubefilter: “Live sports is perhaps the mainstay of modern entertainment. TV and radio engagement may have slipped, but live sports are still going strong on both. And on the internet, leagues, teams, and tournaments have found even deeper connections with their fanbases.”

item.title: New ‘anomaly detector’ flags outlier counties in police uses of lethal force
item.description: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign: “A new data-driven dashboard produced by the Cline Center for Advanced Social Research at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign uses predictive modeling to pinpoint U.S. counties that have unusually high or low numbers of police use of lethal force incidents relative to national benchmarks.”

item.title: The Pergamon Altar is being digitized
item.description: Siemens: “The Pergamon Altar, considered one of the most significant works of Hellenistic art and dating from the 2nd century BC from what is now Turkey, has been one of the central exhibits of the Berlin museum named after it since 1930. The monumental work will soon also be available in an interactive 3D application.”

item.title: Taking experiences with historic collections outside the archive’s walls
item.description: Heritage Fund: “Creating an archive about the fights for disability rights means thinking differently from the start. When we began creating the National Disability Movement Archive and Collection (NDMAC), we knew that preserving history was only part of the job. We also needed to think about how that history and heritage would be collected, who would feel able to contribute and who could access it.”

item.title: Historic discovery finds 19th-century estate agent used peepshow technology to create proto version of Rightmove
item.description: University of Exeter: “A 19th-century estate agent created the world’s first version of Rightmove more than 160 years before the birth of online property previews. Brooks and Green, a high-end estate agent based in Old Bond Street, London, used an early form of immersive visual technology called a cosmorama to offer prospective buyers a virtual tour of the properties they were selling.”

item.title: Vandalized statue of Hiroshima bombings survivor to be revitalized
item.description: King5: “A new statue of Sadako Sasaki is returning to Seattle’s Peace Park, three years after the bronze statue of the historic 12-year-old girl was vandalized, stolen and never recovered. The Sadako Renewal Project, a coalition of Wallingford residents, Asian American artists and local community leaders, plan to unveil and dedicate ‘Sadako: Reimagined’ on Aug. 6, 2027.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Step into the world of tango on Google Arts & Culture
item.description: Google Blog: “Google Arts & Culture has long been committed to preserving and celebrating Argentina’s rich heritage, having collaborated with 25 local partners across the country. Following the success of Argentina’s Table — our exploration of the nation’s diverse culinary scene — we’re now turning our focus to the dance and music style that’s captivated global audiences and earned a place on UNESCO’s Intangible Cultural Heritage list.”

item.title: Historic Ossewabrandwag archive collection enters digital age
item.description: North-West University: “Jacoline Jansen van Vuuren, head of the NWU’s records, archives and museum, says the extensive Ossewabrandwag archive collection has now been fully digitised, ensuring that this significant documentary resource is preserved for future generations while becoming more accessible for research and heritage preservation…. The Ossewabrandwag, which translates to ‘Oxwagon Sentinel’, was an Afrikaner nationalist organisation founded in 1939 and at one stage had more than 350 000 members.”

item.title: CT launches online tool for students to search post-secondary programs
item.description: Connecticut Mirror: “The tool combines enrollment information on approximately 130 colleges, universities and private career centers and more than 4,200 credit and noncredit programs. The programs range from certificates and occupational training through associate’s, bachelor’s, graduate and professional degrees.”

item.title: Celebrate HTML Day 2026 on August 8!
item.description: Aywren’s Nook: “Last year I first discovered HTML day, though this event has now run for the past 4 years! In a day and age when vibe coding is becoming a new reality, the celebration of hand-coded and intentionally built apps and sites is more important than ever.”

item.title: WordPress Security Release 7.0.3 Fixes High Severity XSS Vulnerability
item.description: Search Engine Journal: “WordPress announced a security release 7.0.3 to fix twelve vulnerabilities, three of which appear to be fairly serious, with one vulnerability rated 8.9/10 High.”

item.title: X wants to keep suing advertisers, asks 5th Circuit to overrule district judge
item.description: Ars Technica: “Elon Musk’s X is trying to revive a lawsuit against advertisers it’s accusing of illegally boycotting the social media platform, despite previously reaching a settlement to end litigation against an ad-industry trade group.”

item.title: This Photographer Built An App to Capture Perfect Solar Eclipse Photos
item.description: PetaPixel: “On August 12, 2026, a total solar eclipse will dazzle people in Greenland, Iceland, northern Russia, Spain, and a small part of Portugal, plus some lucky people on boats in the Atlantic Ocean. For photographers gearing up for the total solar eclipse next week, and others farther down the road, photographer Steven Madow has created an incredibly robust new solar eclipse automation app, Umbra.” 100% free!

item.title: Facebook is paying controversial creators to produce rage-bait content
item.description: ABC News (Australia): “An ABC NEWS Verify investigation has found Facebook’s parent company, Meta, is directly paying several controversial content creators including a white nationalist with Neo-Nazi links and a prominent anti-vaxxer. Content produced by these creators appears to be, at times, in direct violation of Facebook’s own policies around content monetisation.”

item.title: Five Interesting Indie Platforms You Might Not Have Heard Of
item.description: Brennan Day: “… in the past couple weeks, I’ve stumbled upon and discovered even more niche websites that I thought I’d share. I don’t think a few would be properly defined as ‘social media’ platforms, but they’re online digital communities of people nonetheless!”

item.title: New Mexico court orders Meta to pay $567 million over mental health harms to kids online
item.description: Associated Press: “A New Mexico court has ordered Instagram and Facebook parent company Meta to pay $567 million to address harms to young people from its platforms in the second phase of a landmark trial. Judge Bryan Biedscheid said in a ruling late Thursday that the bulk of the money — $420 million — will be used for treatment services for young people.”

item.title: US to vet social media of foreign journalists applying for visas, report says
item.description: Reuters: “The report in the conservative news outlet The Daily Signal cited an internal memo that said an initiative by President Donald Trump’s administration that requires applicants for many visa types to make their social media accounts public ​for screening was being expanded to include foreign media representatives.”

item.title: So, theoretically, how much does it cost to buy fake views, followers, comments, likes, and shares right now?
item.description: Tubefilter: “Overall, it found that paying for fakes ‘remains very affordable’ for the average Joe. The most affordable fake? Views, which average $1.40 per 1,000 on TikTok up to $6.70 per 1,000 on YouTube. At the other end of the expense spectrum are comments, which are by far the priciest service.” Good morning, Internet…
